question: Under the TREC-promulgated One to Four Family Residential Contract, the buyer must deliver both the earnest money and the Option Fee to the escrow agent within how many days after the Effective Date?
choice_a: 3 days
choice_b: 10 days
choice_c: 30 days
choice_d: There is no deadline; delivery any time before closing satisfies the contract
explanation: Paragraph 5 (Earnest Money and Termination Option) requires the buyer to deliver both the earnest money and the Option Fee to the escrow agent within 3 days after the Effective Date, with time expressly stated to be of the essence for this deadline.
source_note: TREC One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Paragraph 5

question: When a buyer delivers a single check covering both the Option Fee and the earnest money deposit under the TREC-promulgated contract, the funds received are applied:
choice_a: First to the Option Fee, then to earnest money, then to any additional earnest money
choice_b: First to earnest money, then to the Option Fee
choice_c: Equally split between the Option Fee and earnest money regardless of the amounts specified
choice_d: Entirely to earnest money, with the Option Fee treated as unpaid until a separate check is delivered
explanation: Paragraph 5 directs that funds received from the buyer are applied first to the Option Fee, then to earnest money, then to any additional earnest money, in that order.
source_note: TREC One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Paragraph 5

question: If a buyer properly exercises the unrestricted right to terminate during the Option Period under the TREC-promulgated contract, what generally happens to the Option Fee and the earnest money?
choice_a: The Option Fee is retained by the seller and is not refunded, while the earnest money is refunded to the buyer
choice_b: Both the Option Fee and the earnest money are refunded to the buyer in full
choice_c: Both the Option Fee and the earnest money are forfeited to the seller
choice_d: The earnest money is retained by the seller while the Option Fee is refunded to the buyer
explanation: The Option Fee compensates the seller for taking the property off the market during the option period and is not refunded even if the buyer terminates, while the earnest money -- which secures overall performance -- is refunded to the buyer upon a timely termination during the Option Period.
source_note: TREC One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Paragraph 5

question: If the parties never state a dollar amount for the Option Fee in the TREC-promulgated contract, or the buyer fails to timely deliver it, the buyer:
choice_a: Loses the unrestricted right to terminate the contract during an option period altogether
choice_b: Automatically receives an extended 30-day option period at no cost
choice_c: May still terminate for any reason at any time before closing with no fee owed
choice_d: Forfeits the earnest money immediately regardless of any other contract term
explanation: Paragraph 5 conditions the buyer's unrestricted right to terminate for any reason on stating and timely delivering an Option Fee; without it, that unrestricted termination right does not exist under the contract.
source_note: TREC One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Paragraph 5

question: Under the TREC-promulgated contract's Title Policy and Survey provision, the seller must furnish the title insurance Commitment to the buyer within how many days after the title company receives a copy of the contract?
choice_a: 20 days
choice_b: 3 days
choice_c: 45 days
choice_d: 60 days
explanation: Paragraph 6 requires the seller to furnish the title Commitment within 20 days after the title company receives a copy of the contract; if the deadline is missed, the buyer may ultimately terminate and recover the earnest money.
source_note: TREC One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Paragraph 6

question: If a seller elects to satisfy the survey requirement under the TREC-promulgated contract by furnishing an existing survey rather than a new one, the seller must also provide:
choice_a: A current Residential Real Property Affidavit (T-47 Affidavit) or T-47.1 Declaration confirming no changes since the existing survey
choice_b: A brand-new plat recorded with the county within 24 hours
choice_c: Nothing further; the existing survey alone always satisfies the requirement regardless of the title company's or lender's acceptance
choice_d: A federal flood certification in place of the survey
explanation: The Texas Department of Insurance-promulgated T-47 Affidavit (or T-47.1 Declaration) must accompany an existing survey to confirm no changes have occurred, and if the title company or lender will not accept it, the buyer must obtain a new survey.
source_note: TREC One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Paragraph 6

question: If a buyer timely objects to a title defect under the TREC-promulgated contract and the seller can cure the defect at no cost to the seller, the seller generally has how long to cure before the buyer must decide whether to terminate or waive the objection?
choice_a: 15 days, after which the buyer has 5 days to terminate or waive
choice_b: 60 days, with no further buyer decision period
choice_c: 24 hours only
choice_d: Sellers have no cure period; any valid objection immediately terminates the contract
explanation: Paragraph 6 gives the seller a 15-day Cure Period (only where curing costs the seller nothing), after which the buyer has 5 days to terminate the contract, with earnest money refunded, or waive the objection.
source_note: TREC One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Paragraph 6

question: Under the TREC-promulgated contract's Property Condition paragraph, a buyer's inspector may not perform hydrostatic testing of a home's sewer line unless:
choice_a: The seller has separately authorized hydrostatic testing in writing
choice_b: The buyer has first obtained a court order permitting the test
choice_c: TREC has pre-approved the specific testing company
choice_d: The property is more than 50 years old
explanation: Paragraph 7A requires the seller's separate written authorization before hydrostatic testing may be performed, which is why TREC promulgates a distinct Addendum for Authorizing Hydrostatic Testing to document that consent and allocate risk of any resulting damage.
source_note: TREC One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Paragraph 7A; TREC Addendum for Authorizing Hydrostatic Testing

question: When a TREC-promulgated contract's Property Condition paragraph is checked to accept the property as-is contingent on the seller completing specified repairs, the form specifically warns against:
choice_a: Inserting general phrases such as subject to inspections that fail to identify specific repairs and treatments
choice_b: Listing more than three repairs
choice_c: Requiring the seller to use a licensed contractor
choice_d: Setting any completion deadline for the repairs
explanation: The form expressly cautions that vague, general phrases identifying no specific repair or treatment are insufficient in this as-is-with-repairs option, requiring the parties to specifically identify each repair or treatment the seller must complete.
source_note: TREC One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Paragraph 7D

question: Under the TREC-promulgated contract's Property Condition paragraph, if the cost of lender-required repairs and treatments (including treatment for wood-destroying insects) exceeds a stated percentage of the Sales Price, the buyer may unilaterally terminate the contract and receive a refund of the earnest money. That percentage is:
choice_a: 5% of the Sales Price
choice_b: 10% of the Sales Price
choice_c: 1% of the Sales Price
choice_d: There is no such percentage threshold in the contract
explanation: Paragraph 7E gives the buyer a unilateral right to terminate and recover the earnest money if lender-required repairs and treatments -- which the form explicitly includes wood-destroying insect treatment within -- exceed 5% of the Sales Price.
source_note: TREC One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Paragraph 7E

question: If a seller needs additional time to complete agreed-upon repairs before closing under the TREC-promulgated contract, the Closing Date may generally be extended by up to:
choice_a: 5 days
choice_b: 30 days
choice_c: 90 days
choice_d: The Closing Date can never be extended for repairs under any circumstance
explanation: Paragraph 7F allows the Closing Date to be extended by up to 5 days if needed for the seller, using licensed or otherwise qualified persons, to complete repairs the seller agreed to make.
source_note: TREC One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Paragraph 7F

question: The requirement to disclose known lead-based paint and lead-based paint hazards, referenced in the TREC-promulgated contract's Property Condition paragraph, applies specifically to:
choice_a: Residential dwellings constructed prior to 1978, under federal law
choice_b: All residential dwellings regardless of construction date
choice_c: Only commercial properties
choice_d: Only properties financed with a VA-guaranteed loan
explanation: Federal law (42 U.S.C. Section 4852d) requires disclosure of known lead-based paint and hazards specifically for residential dwellings built before 1978, which TREC's contract and companion lead-based-paint addendum both reference.
source_note: TREC One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Paragraph 7C; 42 U.S.C. Section 4852d

question: A recent addition to the TREC-promulgated contract's Property Condition paragraph requires the seller to provide the buyer with a specific disclosure about:
choice_a: Groundwater and surface water rights associated with the property
choice_b: The seller's personal bankruptcy history
choice_c: The buyer's future property tax exemptions
choice_d: The listing broker's advertising budget
explanation: The current promulgated contract adds a Seller's Disclosure About Groundwater and Surface Water Rights subsection to the Property Condition paragraph, following the same delivery-and-termination-right structure used for the general Seller's Disclosure Notice.
source_note: TREC One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Paragraph 7 (Groundwater and Surface Water Rights)

question: Under the TREC-promulgated contract's Casualty Loss provision, if the property is damaged by fire or other casualty after the Effective Date and the seller cannot restore it to its prior condition by closing due to factors beyond the seller's control, the buyer may generally choose to:
choice_a: Terminate the contract, extend the time for performance up to 15 days, or accept the property with an assignment of insurance proceeds and a closing credit for the deductible
choice_b: Only terminate the contract, with no other option available
choice_c: Only accept the property as-is with no compensation of any kind
choice_d: Force the seller to personally pay for repairs out of pocket regardless of insurance coverage
explanation: Paragraph 14 gives the buyer a choice among three remedies when the seller cannot timely restore casualty-damaged property: terminate and recover earnest money, extend performance up to 15 days, or accept the property with an assignment of insurance proceeds plus a credit equal to the deductible.
source_note: TREC One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Paragraph 14

question: Under the TREC-promulgated contract's Default provision, both a defaulting buyer's forfeited earnest money and a defaulting seller's returned earnest money end up with the non-defaulting party who elects to terminate. A notable textual distinction between these two outcomes is that:
choice_a: Only the seller's recovery of earnest money upon buyer default is expressly labeled liquidated damages in the contract
choice_b: Only the buyer's recovery of earnest money upon seller default is labeled liquidated damages, while the seller's is not
choice_c: Both recoveries are labeled liquidated damages identically
choice_d: Neither recovery uses the term liquidated damages anywhere in the form
explanation: Paragraph 15 expressly labels the seller's recovery of earnest money upon a buyer's default as liquidated damages, but does not apply that same label to the buyer's recovery of earnest money when the seller defaults.
source_note: TREC One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Paragraph 15

question: Under the TREC-promulgated contract's Mediation provision, if a dispute arises and the parties submit it to a mutually acceptable mediation service or provider, the costs of mediation are:
choice_a: Borne equally by the parties
choice_b: Paid entirely by the seller
choice_c: Paid entirely by whichever party requested mediation
choice_d: Paid by the escrow agent out of the earnest money
explanation: Paragraph 16 requires disputing parties to share mediation costs equally, without precluding either party from separately seeking equitable relief from a court.
source_note: TREC One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Paragraph 16

question: The TREC-promulgated contract's Attorney's Fees provision allows reasonable attorney's fees and costs of suit to be recovered by:
choice_a: The prevailing party in a dispute, which may include the buyer, seller, a broker, or the escrow agent
choice_b: Only the buyer, never the seller or any broker
choice_c: Only licensed attorneys who represented a party, regardless of who prevailed
choice_d: No one; each party bears its own attorney's fees under all circumstances
explanation: Paragraph 17 allows the prevailing party -- expressly including the buyer, seller, a broker, or the escrow agent -- to recover reasonable attorney's fees and costs of suit.
source_note: TREC One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Paragraph 17

question: Under the TREC-promulgated contract's Escrow provision, the escrow agent holding the earnest money is generally:
choice_a: Not a party to the contract and not liable for interest on the earnest money held
choice_b: A full party to the contract with the same default remedies available to the buyer or seller
choice_c: Personally liable for interest at the current federal funds rate
choice_d: Required to invest earnest money in an interest-bearing account for the buyer's benefit
explanation: Paragraph 18 provides that the escrow agent is not a party to the contract and is not liable for interest on the earnest money, and is not liable for a depository institution's failure unless that institution is itself the escrow agent.
source_note: TREC One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Paragraph 18

question: At closing, under the TREC-promulgated contract's Escrow provision, earnest money held by the escrow agent is applied:
choice_a: First to any cash down payment, then to the buyer's expenses, with any excess refunded to the buyer
choice_b: First to the broker's commission, with any excess forfeited to the seller
choice_c: Entirely to the seller's proceeds regardless of the buyer's remaining obligations
choice_d: Entirely toward property taxes owed at closing
explanation: Paragraph 18 directs that, at closing, earnest money is applied first to any cash down payment, then to the buyer's expenses, with any remaining excess refunded to the buyer.
source_note: TREC One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Paragraph 18

question: If the contract terminates and only one party makes a written demand to the escrow agent for the earnest money, the TREC-promulgated contract's Escrow provision generally allows the escrow agent to disburse the funds to the demanding party if the other party does not object in writing within:
choice_a: 15 days
choice_b: 3 days
choice_c: 60 days
choice_d: The escrow agent may never disburse without both parties' signatures, regardless of objection
explanation: Paragraph 18's demand procedure requires the escrow agent to notify the non-demanding party, and allows disbursement to the demanding party if no written objection is received within 15 days.
source_note: TREC One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Paragraph 18

question: Under the TREC-promulgated contract's Escrow provision, a party who wrongfully refuses to sign a release of earnest money within a stated period after request is liable to the other party for:
choice_a: Damages, the earnest money, attorney's fees, and costs of suit
choice_b: Nothing, since refusal to sign a release carries no legal consequence
choice_c: Only the amount of the Option Fee
choice_d: Automatic revocation of that party's real estate license
explanation: Paragraph 18 imposes liability -- for damages, the earnest money, attorney's fees, and costs of suit -- on a party who wrongfully refuses to sign a release within 7 days of being requested to do so.
source_note: TREC One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Paragraph 18

question: If a seller under the TREC-promulgated contract is a foreign person under the Internal Revenue Code, or fails to deliver a certificate of non-foreign status, the contract generally requires:
choice_a: The buyer to withhold a portion of the sales proceeds sufficient to comply with federal tax law and deliver it to the IRS
choice_b: The seller's broker to personally pay the seller's federal capital gains tax
choice_c: The transaction to be automatically voided under Texas law
choice_d: TREC to hold the entire sales price in trust indefinitely
explanation: The contract's federal tax requirements provision implements FIRPTA, requiring the buyer to withhold from sales proceeds an amount sufficient to satisfy federal withholding obligations when the seller is a foreign person or fails to certify non-foreign status.
source_note: TREC One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), governmental/federal tax requirements paragraph; Foreign Investment in Real Property Tax Act

question: Under the current TREC-promulgated contract's Notices provision, which of the following is listed as an effective way to deliver notice?
choice_a: Sent by overnight courier
choice_b: Fax transmission, which remains the form's preferred delivery method
choice_c: Verbal notice given over the telephone
choice_d: Posting notice publicly on social media
explanation: The current promulgated form lists mail, hand delivery, overnight courier, and electronic transmission as effective notice methods; a prior version's reference to fax transmission was dropped from the current form's list of effective delivery methods.
source_note: TREC One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Notices paragraph

question: A recent restructuring of the TREC-promulgated contract's Settlement and Other Expenses paragraph added a Brokerage Compensation subsection that expressly states:
choice_a: Brokerage compensation is not set by law and is fully negotiable, structured around seller and/or buyer contributions toward each side's compensation obligations
choice_b: TREC now sets a fixed statewide brokerage commission rate for all transactions
choice_c: Buyers may never contribute toward a seller's broker's compensation under any circumstance
choice_d: Brokerage compensation must always be paid entirely by the seller
explanation: The current contract's Brokerage Compensation subsection states that brokerage compensation is not set by law and is fully negotiable, and structures seller and buyer contributions toward the compensation each side owes its own broker without altering the underlying private compensation agreements.
source_note: TREC One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Settlement and Other Expenses paragraph (Brokerage Compensation)

question: The TREC-promulgated contract's Special Provisions paragraph states it is intended to be used only for informational items, which the form defines as a statement that:
choice_a: Completes a blank in the contract form, discloses factual information, or provides instructions
choice_b: Creates new binding financial obligations between the parties
choice_c: Modifies the default remedies available under the contract
choice_d: Waives any party's statutory right to terminate
explanation: The Special Provisions paragraph defines a permissible informational item as one that completes a blank, discloses factual information, or provides instructions, distinguishing it from substantive contract terms that require an attorney's drafting.
source_note: TREC One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Special Provisions paragraph

question: The TREC-promulgated Third Party Financing Addendum includes checkboxes identifying the specific type of financing the buyer is seeking, including options such as:
choice_a: Conventional, Texas Veterans Loan, FHA insured, VA guaranteed, USDA guaranteed, and reverse mortgage financing
choice_b: Only conventional financing, with no other financing type recognized
choice_c: Cryptocurrency-backed financing exclusively
choice_d: Only seller financing, since third-party financing addenda cannot address government-backed loans
explanation: The Third Party Financing Addendum lets the parties designate the specific loan type sought, including conventional, Texas Veterans Loan, FHA-insured, VA-guaranteed, USDA-guaranteed, and reverse mortgage financing.
source_note: TREC Third Party Financing Addendum

question: The TREC-promulgated Third Party Financing Addendum distinguishes between Buyer Approval (the lender's determination that the buyer qualifies for the loan) and Property Approval (the lender's determination that the property meets underwriting requirements). This distinction matters because:
choice_a: Each has its own separate termination right, and Property Approval's right is tied to a deadline measured by a stated number of days before the Closing Date
choice_b: Only Buyer Approval carries any termination right; Property Approval issues never allow termination
choice_c: The two terms are functionally identical and interchangeable under the addendum
choice_d: Property Approval issues can only be resolved by the seller personally curing them
explanation: The addendum separately addresses Buyer Approval and Property Approval, each with its own termination mechanism; the Property Approval termination right is tied to a deadline expressed as a number of days before the Closing Date, reflecting that appraisal and underwriting issues often surface later in the transaction.
source_note: TREC Third Party Financing Addendum

question: The TREC-promulgated Third Party Financing Addendum's required provision for FHA-insured or VA-guaranteed loans includes a federally mandated appraisal escape clause, which:
choice_a: Relieves the buyer of the obligation to close, without forfeiting earnest money, unless given a written appraisal statement of value not less than a stated amount
choice_b: Requires the buyer to close regardless of the appraised value
choice_c: Allows the seller to unilaterally raise the sales price if the appraisal comes in high
choice_d: Applies equally to all conventional loans, not just FHA or VA financing
explanation: Federal law requires FHA and VA transactions to include an appraisal escape clause relieving the buyer of the obligation to close, without loss of earnest money, unless the buyer is given a written statement of appraised value not less than a stated amount.
source_note: TREC Third Party Financing Addendum, FHA/VA required provision

question: The TREC-promulgated Addendum for Property Subject to Mandatory Membership in a Property Owners Association defines Subdivision Information to include the association's current restrictions, bylaws, and rules, along with:
choice_a: A resale certificate as provided under the Texas Property Code
choice_b: A copy of every past homeowner's personal financial records
choice_c: The developer's original construction blueprints
choice_d: A federal flood insurance policy
explanation: Subdivision Information under this addendum includes a resale certificate as provided under the Texas Property Code, in addition to the association's current restrictions, bylaws, and rules.
source_note: Texas Property Code Section 207.003; TREC Addendum for Property Subject to Mandatory Membership in a Property Owners Association

question: The TREC-promulgated Addendum for Property Subject to Mandatory Membership in a Property Owners Association allows the parties to cap the buyer's exposure to association transfer fees, deposits, and reserves at a stated dollar amount, with:
choice_a: The seller responsible for paying any amount exceeding that stated cap
choice_b: The buyer always responsible for the full amount regardless of any cap
choice_c: The escrow agent personally absorbing any excess
choice_d: No mechanism to cap or allocate these fees at all
explanation: The addendum caps the buyer's exposure to association transfer fees, deposits, and reserves at a stated dollar figure, with the seller responsible for paying any amount above that cap.
source_note: TREC Addendum for Property Subject to Mandatory Membership in a Property Owners Association

question: The TREC-promulgated Seller's Temporary Residential Lease and Buyer's Temporary Residential Lease differ in that:
choice_a: The Seller's Temporary Residential Lease is used only when the seller occupies the property for up to 90 days after closing, with the buyer as landlord, while the Buyer's Temporary Residential Lease is used only when the buyer occupies the property for up to 90 days before closing, with the seller as landlord
choice_b: Both leases are used only after closing, with the seller always acting as landlord
choice_c: Both leases have no time limit on occupancy
choice_d: The Buyer's Temporary Residential Lease is used only when the seller occupies the property
explanation: The two temporary lease addenda serve opposite occupancy scenarios, each capped at 90 days: the Seller's Temporary Residential Lease covers post-closing seller occupancy (buyer as landlord, seller as tenant), while the Buyer's Temporary Residential Lease covers pre-closing buyer occupancy (seller as landlord, buyer as tenant).
source_note: TREC Seller's Temporary Residential Lease; TREC Buyer's Temporary Residential Lease

question: The TREC-promulgated Buyer's Temporary Residential Lease, used when a buyer takes early occupancy before closing, includes a notice specifically clarifying that:
choice_a: The lease deposit must be in addition to the earnest money required under the sales contract
choice_b: The lease deposit and the earnest money are the same funds and may not be collected separately
choice_c: No deposit of any kind may be collected under a buyer's temporary lease
choice_d: The lease deposit automatically satisfies the buyer's Option Fee obligation
explanation: The Buyer's Temporary Residential Lease expressly notes that its deposit must be in addition to the earnest money under the sales contract, keeping the two funds legally and functionally separate.
source_note: TREC Buyer's Temporary Residential Lease

question: The TREC-promulgated Short Sale Addendum applies when a seller's anticipated net proceeds are insufficient to pay off the existing mortgage, making the contract contingent on:
choice_a: Obtaining the mortgage lienholder's consent to accept the net proceeds in full satisfaction of the debt and deliver a recordable lien release
choice_b: The buyer obtaining a personal loan from the seller's own lender
choice_c: The seller declaring personal bankruptcy first
choice_d: TREC's prior written approval of the specific sale
explanation: The Short Sale Addendum conditions the contract on the lienholder's consent to accept the net sale proceeds in full satisfaction of the debt and to deliver a recordable release of its lien.
source_note: TREC Short Sale Addendum

question: Under the TREC-promulgated Short Sale Addendum, once the seller notifies the buyer that the lienholder's consent has been obtained, the contract's:
choice_a: Effective Date is changed to that notice date, an Amended Effective Date, for purposes of measuring further performance deadlines
choice_b: Sales price is automatically reduced to the lienholder's payoff amount
choice_c: Earnest money is immediately forfeited to the seller
choice_d: Closing must occur within 24 hours regardless of any other deadline
explanation: The Short Sale Addendum resets the contract's Effective Date to the date of the seller's notice that lienholder consent was obtained, establishing an Amended Effective Date from which remaining performance deadlines are measured.
source_note: TREC Short Sale Addendum

question: The TREC-promulgated Addendum for Back-Up Contract makes a new contract binding upon execution but contingent on:
choice_a: Termination of a prior, first contract by a stated date, after which the seller's notice of that termination amends the Back-Up Contract's Effective Date
choice_b: The buyer first closing on an unrelated property
choice_c: A minimum six-month waiting period before any earnest money is due
choice_d: TREC's formal registration of the back-up status
explanation: A Back-Up Contract is binding when signed but is contingent on the prior, first contract terminating by a stated date; once the seller notifies the buyer of that termination, the Back-Up Contract's Effective Date is amended to that notice date, and additional earnest money and Option Fee become due.
source_note: TREC Addendum for Back-Up Contract

question: The TREC-promulgated Addendum Concerning Right to Terminate Due to Lender's Appraisal is used only when the Third Party Financing Addendum is attached and the loan is not FHA-insured or VA-guaranteed, because:
choice_a: FHA and VA financing already carry their own statutory appraisal escape clause within the Third Party Financing Addendum's required provisions
choice_b: FHA and VA loans never require an appraisal
choice_c: TREC prohibits any appraisal-related addendum on government-backed loans
choice_d: Conventional loans never require an appraisal, making the addendum unnecessary for them
explanation: Because FHA and VA financing already carry a statutory appraisal escape clause built into the Third Party Financing Addendum's required provisions, the separate lender's-appraisal termination addendum is used only for non-FHA/VA financing.
source_note: TREC Addendum Concerning Right to Terminate Due to Lender's Appraisal

question: The TREC-promulgated Addendum for Authorizing Hydrostatic Testing requires that the testing be performed by:
choice_a: A licensed plumber, at the buyer's expense, with the parties allocating responsibility for any resulting damage
choice_b: Any unlicensed handyman the buyer chooses
choice_c: The seller personally, at no cost to the buyer
choice_d: A TREC-certified inspector, since plumbers are not permitted to perform this test
explanation: The addendum authorizes a licensed plumber, engaged at the buyer's expense, to perform the hydrostatic test, while the parties allocate through checkboxes who bears responsibility for any resulting damage.
source_note: TREC Addendum for Authorizing Hydrostatic Testing

question: The TREC-promulgated Environmental Assessment, Threatened or Endangered Species, and Wetlands Addendum provides for three separately checkable authorizations, covering:
choice_a: An environmental assessment report, a threatened or endangered species report, and a wetlands report
choice_b: Only a single combined environmental report covering all issues at once
choice_c: Only threatened species issues, since environmental contamination is addressed elsewhere
choice_d: Only wetlands issues on properties within one mile of the coast
explanation: This addendum lets the parties independently authorize an environmental assessment report, a threatened or endangered species report, and a wetlands report, each triggering its own buyer termination right if an adverse report is furnished.
source_note: TREC Environmental Assessment, Threatened or Endangered Species, and Wetlands Addendum

question: The TREC-promulgated Addendum for Property Located Seaward of the Gulf Intracoastal Waterway, grounded in Texas Natural Resources Code Section 61.025, is distinct from the separate Addendum for Coastal Area Property because it specifically addresses:
choice_a: The Open Beaches Act erosion risk that structures may end up seaward of the vegetation line and become subject to a state-ordered removal action
choice_b: Only homeowners association dues owed on beachfront lots
choice_c: Only flood insurance premium calculations
choice_d: Only the property's proximity to a public boat ramp
explanation: This addendum warns that Gulf coastline erosion can place structures seaward of the natural vegetation line, subjecting them to a state lawsuit ordering removal at the owner's expense, a distinctly different concern from the separate Coastal Area Property addendum's tidal-boundary and fill-disclosure focus.
source_note: Texas Natural Resources Code Section 61.025; TREC Addendum for Property Located Seaward of the Gulf Intracoastal Waterway

question: The TREC-promulgated Addendum for Reservation of Oil, Gas, and Other Minerals defines Mineral Estate broadly to include oil, gas, and other minerals along with associated rights, but expressly excludes:
choice_a: Water, sand, gravel, limestone, building stone, caliche, surface shale, near-surface lignite, and iron
choice_b: All hydrocarbons of any kind, making the addendum meaningless for oil and gas
choice_c: Royalty interests, which are always conveyed to the buyer regardless of any reservation
choice_d: Executive rights, which can never be reserved by a seller
explanation: The addendum's definition of Mineral Estate specifically excludes water, sand, gravel, limestone, building stone, caliche, surface shale, near-surface lignite, and iron, distinguishing them from the oil, gas, and other minerals a seller may reserve.
source_note: TREC Addendum for Reservation of Oil, Gas, and Other Minerals

question: Under the TREC-promulgated Addendum for Reservation of Oil, Gas, and Other Minerals, if the parties fail to check a box indicating whether the seller retains or waives rights of ingress and egress for mining or drilling, the form:
choice_a: Deems this a waiver, meaning the seller is treated as having elected to convey all surface rights to the buyer
choice_b: Deems this an automatic retention of full surface access rights by the seller
choice_c: Voids the entire mineral reservation
choice_d: Requires the transaction to be delayed until the box is checked, with no default rule
explanation: If neither ingress/egress option is checked, the addendum deems the seller to have elected to convey all surface rights, meaning an unchecked box defaults against the seller retaining surface access for mining or drilling.
source_note: TREC Addendum for Reservation of Oil, Gas, and Other Minerals

question: The TREC-promulgated Addendum for Sale of Other Property by Buyer conditions the contract on the buyer's receipt of proceeds from selling another property. If the seller receives a competing offer and forces the buyer to waive that contingency, a buyer who then fails to close solely because those proceeds were never received:
choice_a: Is in default under the contract and subject to the seller's default remedies
choice_b: Automatically receives an extension with no consequence
choice_c: Can never be found in default regardless of the reason for non-closing
choice_d: Is entitled to a full refund of earnest money regardless of the waiver
explanation: The addendum conditions the contract on the buyer's actual receipt of sale proceeds, not merely closing on the other property, and once the buyer waives that contingency in response to a competing offer, a resulting failure to close exposes the buyer to the seller's default remedies.
source_note: TREC Addendum for Sale of Other Property by Buyer

question: The TREC-promulgated Addendum for Property in a Propane Gas System Service Area, grounded in the Texas Utilities Code, functions as:
choice_a: A pure notice acknowledgment, requiring the buyer to acknowledge receipt of the retailer's recorded notice, without creating any contract contingency
choice_b: A financing contingency allowing termination if propane costs exceed a stated amount
choice_c: A repair-cost allocation addendum for propane tank replacement
choice_d: A mandatory arbitration clause specific to propane disputes
explanation: Under Texas Utilities Code Section 141.010, this addendum is purely a notice-acknowledgment form, requiring the buyer to acknowledge receipt of the propane distribution system retailer's recorded notice, with no contingency or termination right built into the addendum itself.
source_note: Texas Utilities Code Section 141.010; TREC Addendum for Property in a Propane Gas System Service Area

question: Under the TREC-promulgated Loan Assumption Addendum, after the buyer delivers required credit documentation, the seller generally has a stated number of days to reject the buyer's creditworthiness in the seller's sole discretion, and the addendum separately flags the risk that:
choice_a: The existing noteholder's due-on-sale clause could allow the lender to accelerate the full loan balance if the lender does not consent to the assumption
choice_b: The buyer automatically becomes personally liable for the seller's original loan origination fees
choice_c: TREC must individually approve every loan assumption before closing
choice_d: Loan assumptions are prohibited on any loan originated after 2000
explanation: The Loan Assumption Addendum warns that an assumed loan's due-on-sale clause could let the noteholder accelerate the full balance if it does not consent to the assumption, in addition to giving the seller a discretionary window to reject the buyer's submitted creditworthiness.
source_note: TREC Loan Assumption Addendum

question: The TREC-promulgated Addendum for Seller's Disclosure of Information on Lead-Based Paint and Lead-Based Paint Hazards gives a buyer who elects to inspect (rather than waive inspection) a period after the Effective Date to have the property inspected, and a separate, longer period within which to terminate in writing if lead-based paint or hazards are found; these periods are, respectively:
choice_a: 10 days to inspect and 14 days to terminate
choice_b: 30 days to inspect and 10 days to terminate
choice_c: The same single 10-day period for both inspecting and terminating
choice_d: 3 days to inspect and 3 days to terminate
explanation: The addendum gives a buyer who elects to inspect 10 days after the Effective Date to complete the inspection, but a separate, longer 14-day window after the Effective Date to give written notice of termination if lead-based paint or hazards are found.
source_note: TREC Addendum for Seller's Disclosure of Information on Lead-Based Paint and Lead-Based Paint Hazards

question: The TREC-promulgated Addendum for Seller's Disclosure of Information on Lead-Based Paint and Lead-Based Paint Hazards requires brokers to retain a completed copy of the addendum for:
choice_a: At least 3 years following the sale
choice_b: 30 days following the sale
choice_c: The broker's entire licensure period with no defined end
choice_d: There is no retention requirement for brokers under this addendum
explanation: The addendum requires brokers to retain a completed copy for at least 3 years following the sale, consistent with federal recordkeeping expectations for lead-based paint disclosures.
source_note: TREC Addendum for Seller's Disclosure of Information on Lead-Based Paint and Lead-Based Paint Hazards
